headline: Massachusetts says it has no DEA guidance before 29 November
dek: Massachusetts' cannabis regulator told licensees on 18 November it has no federal guidance on DEA registration, 11 days before the DEA's supply-chain deadline.
key_points: Massachusetts' Cannabis Control Commission said in an 18 November bulletin that no federal agency has given it implementation guidance on Schedule III medical cannabis or DEA registration.
The commission shared the DEA's timely-applicant notice with licensees but said it cannot interpret federal rules or give legal, tax or business advice; state rules are unchanged.
The DEA notice gives pending applicants until 29 November to trade only with other applicants or registrants, with a narrow exception for testing at non-DEA labs in the same state.
In Hawaii, Senate health chair Joy San Buenaventura said rescheduling may clear the way for a law letting some patients use medical cannabis in hospitals.
body: Massachusetts has told its cannabis businesses that, as far as federal rescheduling goes, they are on their own. In a bulletin dated 18 November, the state's Cannabis Control Commission (CCC) said it has not received implementation guidance from any federal agency about the DEA's registration process for Schedule III medical cannabis, and that it cannot advise licensees on how the federal requirements apply to them.

The bulletin, signed by Executive Director Travis Ahern and addressed to both adult-use marijuana establishments and medical marijuana treatment centers, arrives 11 days before the DEA's 29 November deadline for pending applicants to rebuild their supply chains around federally recognised partners. Massachusetts licenses both adult-use and medical businesses, which puts it among the dual-licence states whose place in the federal system is least certain.

The CCC said it continues to monitor federal developments and shared, for information only, the DEA's notice on timely applicants for medical marijuana registration. It stressed that enforcing federal cannabis law is outside its jurisdiction and that it cannot give legal, tax or business advice about the impact on any licensee. Businesses should consult their own lawyers and advisers, the bulletin said.

The commission also said the federal changes do not, for now, alter how it administers state law. Licensees remain bound by Massachusetts' cannabis statutes, chapters 94G and 94I of the General Laws, and by the commission's regulations at 935 CMR 500 and 501. In plain terms: a business can be compliant in Massachusetts and still face open questions about its federal status, and the state regulator will not resolve those questions for it.
> State regulators are now telling operators what the DEA has not: nobody in Boston can say how the federal rules apply to them.

The DEA document the CCC circulated sets out what applicants who filed complete applications between 28 April and 26 June 2026 may do while they wait for a decision. Under 21 CFR 1301.13(k)(7), these timely applicants can keep dispensing, manufacturing or distributing Schedule III medical marijuana under their state licences.

But they may deal only with other timely applicants and with DEA registrants. Trading with anyone else, including state-licensed businesses that never applied, could be grounds for denying an application or revoking a registration, the DEA said. The agency expects applicants to complete due diligence on every trading partner: collecting the DEA submission confirmation, checking the partner's document control number on the DEA Diversion Control website, obtaining copies of registrations and active state licences, and keeping records of all of it. The deadline to establish compliant supply chains is 29 November 2026. Inventory acquired before the notice, even from non-qualifying sources, may still be sold.

Testing gets a narrow exception. Many states require samples to go to state-licensed labs, and few labs hold DEA registrations. The DEA said it does not intend to penalise applicants or registrants for sending small, de minimis quantities to a non-registered lab in the same state, with detailed records, but only where using a DEA-registered lab would break state law: either because no lab anywhere in the country is registered, or because state law bars out-of-state testing and no in-state lab is registered. Product may not come back from such a lab. The notice says it does not have the force of law.

As we reported on 16 November, the Cannabis Regulators Association said the DEA guidance has split most state medical markets into a federal track and a state-only track, and that regulators have had no substantive engagement from the agency. The CCC bulletin puts that gap in writing, from one of the largest adult-use states, to its own licensees. The DEA has already moved against dual-licence operators elsewhere: as we reported on 12 November, it sent orders to show cause to medical businesses in California, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Illinois, North Dakota and Oregon, partly on the argument that letting the same businesses sell adult-use cannabis breaks the federal closed system.

For Massachusetts treatment centers, many of which also hold adult-use licences, that history makes the next ten days a practical problem. They must decide whom they can buy from and sell to under the DEA notice without help from the regulator that licenses them. For information on who has applied, the CCC could point licensees only to the DEA's own published material.

Rescheduling is also feeding new state proposals. Hawaii Sen. Joy San Buenaventura, who chairs the Senate Health and Human Services Committee, told The Marijuana Herald that Schedule III status appears to remove obstacles to a Ryan's Law, which would let certain patients keep using medical cannabis while in health care facilities. She said she has no specific bill in mind yet.

Hawaii's SB 2408, which she cosponsored this year, would have allowed terminally ill patients and qualifying patients over 65 with chronic illness to use medical cannabis in specified facilities. It passed the Senate 25 to 0 on 10 March but stalled in the House Judiciary and Hawaiian Affairs Committee on 1 April, according to the Herald. She also wants protections for patients in child custody disputes and floated legalising low-potency cannabis if broader legalisation fails. Virginia, as we reported this morning, has already finalised rules letting hospital staff administer medical cannabis from 16 December.

The DEA's 29 November deadline is the next test: watch whether Massachusetts operators shift suppliers, whether the CCC issues further notices, and whether the DEA sends show-cause orders to Massachusetts dual licensees as it did in six other jurisdictions. In Hawaii, watch for a Ryan's Law bill when the 2027 session opens. In Virginia, hospital administration of medical cannabis begins on 16 December.
